description_full: Church & Dwight Co., Inc. develops, manufactures, and markets household, personal care, and specialty products. It operates in three segments: Consumer Domestic, Consumer International, and Specialty Products Division. The company offers baking soda, cat litters, laundry detergents, carpet deodorizers, and other baking soda-based products under the ARM & HAMMER brand; stain removers, cleaning solutions, laundry detergents, and bleach alternatives under the OXICLEAN brand; dry shampoos under the BATISTE brand; water flossers under the WATERPIK brand; oral care products under the THERABREATH brand; acne treatment products under the HERO brand; hand sanitizers under the TOUCHLAND brand; and condoms, lubricants, and vibrators under the TROJAN brand. It also provides home pregnancy and ovulation test kits under the FIRST RESPONSE brand; depilatories under the NAIR; oral analgesics under the ORAJEL brand; laundry detergents under the XTRA brand; and cold shortening and relief products under the ZICAM brand. In addition, the company's specialty products include animal and food productivity products, such as ARM & HAMMER baking soda as a feed additive to help dairy cow; BIO-CHLOR and FERMENTEN used to reduce health issues associated with calving, as well as needed protein; CELMANAX refined functional carbohydrate, a yeast-based prebiotic; and CERTILLUS a probiotics products used in the poultry, dairy, beef, and swine industries. Additionally, it offers sodium bicarbonate; and cleaning and deodorizing products. The company sells its consumer products through supermarkets, mass merchandisers, wholesale clubs, drugstores, convenience stores, home stores, dollar and other discount stores, pet and other specialty stores, websites and other e-commerce channels; and specialty products to industrial customers and livestock producers through distributors. Church & Dwight Co., Inc. was founded in 1846 and is headquartered in Ewing, New Jersey.

financial_summary: Church & Dwight Company, Inc. is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $26.7B market cap on $6.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 7% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 45%.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.65× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 11.3×.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 1% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $102 (margin of safety -11%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 40%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $75.51 to $140 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 34.7 vs 18.3, EV/EBITDA 20.3 vs 10.2 and P/FCF 24.4 vs 16.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 33% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 18 covering analysts target $110 on average, 2% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 14% clears the cost of capital of 6.6% by 7pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.18).
It runs a 45% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.65x.
ROE of 18% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.3% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($409.0M of cash against $2.2B of debt), with interest covered 11.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.4, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.9% over 3 years, 4.8% over 5 years and 6.2% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 4.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (2.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 7.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $14.9M sold).
It returns 4.5% a year to shareholders (3.4% in buybacks and 1.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 35 consecutive years, raising it 3.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 5,550 employees, each generates about $1.1M of revenue, 2.2x the Consumer Defensive median, and revenue has grown 6.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $197K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
